biodiversity-s2.title: A seal population that came back
biodiversity-s2.html:
By the 1890s, hunting for their oil had cut northern elephant seals down to one small colony, perhaps a few dozen animals, on an island off the coast of Mexico. Once hunting stopped, the colony grew, and today more than 200,000 of these seals breed along the coasts of Mexico and California. Researchers compared DNA from living seals with DNA from museum skins collected before the hunting began. The living seals carry far less genetic variety than their ancestors did. A comeback in numbers, the researchers argue, can hide a loss that lasts: a population descended from so few survivors may cope poorly with a new disease or a change in its ocean.

Invented passage for practice, summarizing published studies of northern elephant seals (DNA from museum specimens; population counts near 225,000 in 2010).

ecosystem-services-s1.title: A city keeps its forest
ecosystem-services-s1.html:
Riverton draws its drinking water from a reservoir in hills 80 kilometers away. As houses and farms spread into those hills, state regulators warned that the city would have to build a filtration plant costing about $6 billion, plus $250 million a year to run it. The city chose a different plan. It spent $1.5 billion over ten years to buy land near the reservoir, to pay farmers to fence cattle away from streams, and to repair failing septic tanks. Forest soils filter rainwater as it soaks in, and roots hold soil in place so less mud reaches the reservoir. Ten years later the water still meets drinking standards without filtration. Some upstream towns complain that the land purchases limit where they can build and shrink their tax income.

Invented passage for practice, modeled on real cities that protect forested land around their reservoirs.

succession-s2.title: Life returns to a volcano
succession-s2.html:
In May 1980, Mount St. Helens in Washington State erupted. The blast flattened 600 square kilometers of forest, and a fan of hot rock and ash on the volcano’s north side, later named the Pumice Plain, buried the ground under many meters of fresh rock. On the Pumice Plain, nothing survived; a few years later only scattered plants had arrived. Farther out, where the blast knocked trees down but left soil, roots and buried seeds, plants sprouted the first summer, and pocket gophers dug fresh soil up to the surface. Ecologists who have studied both areas since 1980 report that life returned much faster where soil remained than on the rock of the Pumice Plain.

Invented passage for practice, summarizing USGS accounts and published research at Mount St. Helens.

items.q: Build the cause-and-effect chain that explains why sea otters are called a keystone species.

specific.frame: When sea otters are removed, ___, so ___, which ___.

cause.label: First effect
options: sea urchin numbers increase
kelp grows faster
sea urchins starve
fish eat more kelp

why.1: Kelp is eaten by urchins; it does not gain from losing otters directly.
why.2: Urchins lose their predator, so they survive and multiply rather than starve.
why.3: Fish shelter in kelp; the urchins are the grazers that matter here.

effect.label: Second effect
options: urchins graze the kelp forest down
urchins leave the coast
kelp forests spread to deeper water

why.1: With more food and no predator, urchins stay and graze.
why.2: More urchins means less kelp, not more.

mechanism.label: Result for the community
options: removes the habitat many fish and invertebrates depend on
adds food for the fish that live in kelp
has no effect beyond the urchins

why.1: Losing kelp takes away food and shelter; it does not add food.
why.2: The change spreads through the community; that is why otters are called keystone.

specific.model: When sea otters are removed, sea urchin numbers increase, so the urchins graze the kelp forest down, which removes the habitat that many fish depend on.

apples ripen earlier
the trees need less water

items.q: Build the chain that explains why a small forest fragment surrounded by farmland loses species over time.

specific.frame: Because the fragment is small, ___. Because farmland surrounds it, ___. So ___.

cause.label: Effect of small size
options: its populations are small and easily wiped out
it receives more sunlight than a large forest
its trees grow faster

why.1: Sunlight is not how size changes the number of species.
why.2: Tree growth rate does not explain the loss of species.

effect.label: Effect of isolation
options: few individuals of lost species can arrive to replace them
more species arrive from the farms
predators cannot enter the fragment

why.1: Most forest species cannot live on or cross farmland, so fewer arrive, not more.
why.2: Predators can still enter; isolation mostly blocks recolonization.

mechanism.label: Result
options: the number of species in the fragment decreases
the number of species in the fragment increases
the species become more genetically diverse

why.1: More losses and fewer arrivals lower the count.
why.2: Small, isolated populations lose genetic diversity rather than gain it.

specific.model: Because the fragment is small, its populations are small and easily wiped out. Because farmland surrounds it, few individuals of lost species can arrive to replace them. So the number of species in the fragment decreases.

keeps the population the same size

why.2: Fewer births and lower survival change the population size.

specific.model: At 22 °C the trout are in a zone of physiological stress, so individuals feed, grow and reproduce less, which lowers births and survival, so the population decreases.

items.q: Explain how a severe drought can lower the number of frogs in a wetland.

cause.label: Change in the wetland
options: shallow pools dry up
the water gets colder
more insects hatch

why.1: Drought brings less water; it does not make the water colder.
why.2: More insects would be food for frogs, not a cause of decline.

effect.label: Effect on frogs
options: frogs have fewer places to lay eggs and tadpoles die before they change into frogs
frogs lay more eggs in deeper water
frogs grow larger

why.1: Deep water is scarcer in a drought, not more common.
why.2: Body size is not the main effect of losing water.

mechanism.label: Effect on the population
options: lowers the number of young frogs, so the population decreases
raises the number of young frogs
has no effect on the population

why.1: Losing breeding pools lowers the number of young.
why.2: Losing breeding habitat changes how many young survive.

specific.model: During a drought, shallow pools dry up, so frogs have fewer places to lay eggs and tadpoles die before they change into frogs, which lowers the number of young frogs, so the population decreases.

items.q: Explain how bacteria in a hospital become resistant to an antibiotic over many generations.

specific.frame: A few bacteria ___. When the antibiotic is used, ___, so ___.

cause.label: Starting variation
options: already carry a trait that lets them survive the drug
decide to change in order to survive the drug
are all identical to one another

why.1: Bacteria do not change on purpose; resistant ones were already present.
why.2: If all were identical, the drug would kill all of them, and nothing would be selected.

effect.label: Selection
options: the resistant ones survive while most others die
every bacterium dies equally
the drug makes every bacterium stronger

why.1: If all died equally, there would be no change in the population’s traits.
why.2: The drug does not strengthen bacteria; it removes the ones it can kill.

mechanism.label: Result
options: the resistant bacteria multiply and resistance becomes common in later generations
the population returns to how it was before
resistance disappears from the population

why.1: The survivors are mostly resistant, so their offspring are too.
why.2: Selection raised resistance; it did not remove it.

specific.model: A few bacteria already carry a trait that lets them survive the drug. When the antibiotic is used, the resistant ones survive while most others die, so the resistant bacteria multiply and resistance becomes common in later generations.

items.q: Explain why secondary succession is faster than primary succession.

specific.frame: In secondary succession, ___ are already present, while primary succession must first ___, so ___.

cause.label: What remains
options: soil, seeds and roots
large mature trees
bare rock and ash

why.1: Mature trees are usually removed by the disruption.
why.2: Bare rock is the start of primary succession, not secondary.

effect.label: Extra step in primary
options: build soil from bare rock, which takes centuries
wait for a fire to clear the land
remove the soil that is already there

why.1: Primary succession does not need a fire; it needs soil.
why.2: There is no soil to remove in primary succession.

mechanism.label: Result
options: plants can grow sooner in secondary succession
primary succession reaches a mature forest first
both take the same time

why.1: Primary succession is slower because soil must form first.
why.2: Building soil adds a long first step to primary succession.

specific.model: In secondary succession, soil, seeds and roots are already present, while primary succession must first build soil from bare rock, which takes centuries, so plants can grow sooner in secondary succession.
